newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan supermarket chief arrested in DKB scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan supermarket chief arrested in DKB scandal.

text.p: The head of major Japanese supermarket chain Jusco Co was arrested on Tuesday for his previous links to a racketeer payoff scandal involving Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.

In another wrenching day for one of Japan's top banks, four former executives including Kenji Tanaka, now president of Jusco, were arrested and half of DKB's 40 board members resigned in a shakeup which included naming a new president.
The affair has also ensnared Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd. There was no suggestion that Jusco itself was involved in the scandal.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto hinted that DKB's role as the sole bank for the country's national lottery, a lucrative source of funds, might also be reviewed because of the scandal.
"We have to secure the impartiality of the lottery sales process, but I am not sure if one entity should monopolize it," Hashimoto told parliament on Tuesday.

Tokyo prosecutors said they arrested former DKB vice presidents Akira Kanazawa and Tsuneo Uchida as well as former managing directors Tanaka and Yasuyuki Terasawa, on suspicion of violating the Commercial Code with payoffs in the form of illicit loans to a "sokaiya" racketeer.
Sokaiya extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings.
The 39 loans, totalling 8.8 billion yen ($77.8 million), were allegedly made from 1994 to 1996 through Daiwa Shinyo, a non-bank financial institution affiliated with DKB.
The four former executives were responsible at the time for screening the bank's loans for irregularities.

The scandal, which has now led to the arrests of 14 people, including four other DKB officials and a former Nomura president, is unfolding just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms of its long-protected financial sector.
The fresh arrests came just after the bank announced a new executive line-up which it said was untainted by the affair.

DKB, Japan's second biggest bank in terms of deposits, already has scrapped one management reshuffle in a bid to clean up an affair it says involved loans to Yoshinori Koike, younger brother of Ryuichi Koike, a sokaiya at the heart of the scandal.

DKB said on Tuesday that managing director Katsuyuki Sugita, 54, would take over as president on June 27. Twenty-one of the bank's 40 directors, including chairman Tadashi Okuda, president Katsuhiko Kondo and Fujita, will step down.
"It is extremely regrettable that the scandal has lowered our credibility as a bank and as a company," DKB said.
New DKB president Sugita promised on Tuesday a wholesale overhaul of the bank's corporate culture.
"I will make today the day of DKB's rebirth," Sugita told a news conference.

DKB, which like Nomura is suffering customer defections and possible stiff penalties, said it would implement reforms to prevent any future misdeeds, including creation of a committee of outside auditors to check for dubious business activities.
Authorities are believed to want to make an example of DKB and Nomura to teach others a lesson in corporate ethics.
But some experts say the old ways cannot be completely erased until much of the current generation of top executives at financial institutions relinquishes power.
"We're dealing with an entire generation who has to go into retirement before conduct really changes," one financial industry source said.

Nomura, which ran into the same trouble in 1991, has been indicted for violating securities law by illegally compensating a firm run by Yoshinori Koike. Two ex-Nomura directors have been indicted and former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki arrested.
Nomura has already effected its own management reshuffle, promoting Junichi Unjiie, a 51-year-old corporate youngster with a University of Chicago doctorate, to president.
